titulo: Πού είναι — and the answer that fits in your head
subtitulo: Five places, one opening, and a follow-up short enough to be answered with a hand
cena: A corner in the centre of Athens: five streets, two of them signed, and the place you want is somewhere behind one of them.
frasePiso: Πού είναι, then the place, exactly as the map spells it. Then shrink the answer until it fits in your head.

clique.desconto: Nobody gave you a separate question for each of those. You kept one opening and dropped in the word you had already read off the map.
clique.piso: Next time you are lost, you will not open a paragraph. You will ask two words, then narrow the answer down to a hand pointing.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Greek place names on road signs are romanised by the national standard ELOT 743, second edition 2001, identical to ISO 843:1997. The British PCGN records that it «is very widely used on road signs in Greece as well as printed guide books», that «place names in Wikipedia and on Google Earth are not romanized consistently», and — the part that matters at a corner — that ELOT 743 «is a less reliable guide to Modern Greek pronunciation» than the older system it replaced. Reading the sign aloud does not produce the Greek word.

ΕΛΟΤ 743, 2ª edição, 2001, idêntica à ISO 843:1997.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Politeness in Greek and in English is documented as running on opposite defaults: Greek is oriented to positive politeness — involvement and closeness — and English to negative politeness — distance and non-imposition. The symmetrical consequence is documented too: the English speaker reads the Greek as abrupt or intrusive, and the Greek reads the English speaker as cold. Both readings are artefacts of the mismatch.
fatosDatados.fonte: Maria Sifianou, Politeness Phenomena in England and Greece; Bayraktaroğlu & Sifianou (eds.), Linguistic Politeness Across Boundaries, John Benjamins, P&BNS 88. Panorama recente: Languages, 2026, doi:10.3390/languages11050107.

steps.pt: Ask where something is and you can get a paragraph back. The trick is asking so the answer fits in your head.
Here is the frame: Πού είναι, then the place. The place goes in exactly as the map spells it.
Where is the bus stop?

steps.promptPt: The app says the bus leaves in four minutes and there is no shelter in sight. Ask the man at the kiosk. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the bus stop?

steps.es: Ευθεία και μετά δεξιά, δίπλα στο περίπτερο.
steps.pt: Straight on and then right, next to the kiosk.
steps.tts: Ευθεία και μετά δεξιά, δίπλα στο περίπτερο.
steps.acao: Two moves and a landmark. Take the first move now and ask again when you get there.

steps.pt: Nothing changes shape after Πού είναι. You read the word on the map, and you say the word.

steps.promptPt: You are in a station hall with four stairways and none of them is signed in a way you can read. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the exit?
Road signs are romanised by a standard used very widely in Greece — and it is a poor guide to the sound.
So say the Greek, not the sign. ΒΟΛΟΣ is Volos, not Bolos: that Β is a V, and the Η is an ee.

steps.promptPt: You are inside a café, you have already ordered, and there is one door at the back with no picture on it. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the toilet?

steps.promptPt: Your blister has gone from annoying to limping, and you want the green cross on this street. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the pharmacy?

steps.promptPt: You got off the train at Piraeus, everyone is walking in three directions, and your boat leaves at eight. Speak now.
steps.pt: Where is the port?

steps.es: Πέντε λεπτά με τα πόδια. Ακολουθήστε τον κόσμο.
steps.pt: Five minutes on foot. Follow the crowd.
steps.tts: Πέντε λεπτά με τα πόδια. Ακολουθήστε τον κόσμο.
steps.acao: A time and an instruction, no street names at all. That is a complete answer — take it.

steps.pt: Now shrink the answer. Far or not, left or right, this way — three words and a pointed finger.

steps.promptPt: They have just pointed down a long street and you need to know whether to walk it or find a bus. Speak now.
steps.pt: Is it far?

steps.promptPt: The answer had four street names in it and you caught none of them. Offer them two options instead. Speak now.
steps.pt: Left or right?
Research describes Greek politeness as leaning on closeness where English leans on distance. Short reads as normal.

steps.promptPt: You are stopping a stranger mid-stride on the pavement, and the machine you need takes cards. Speak now.
steps.pt: Excuse me, where is the cash machine?

steps.promptPt: At the hotel desk, your phone is at six percent and paper survives a flat battery. Speak now.
steps.pt: Do you have a map?

steps.es: Ναι, ορίστε. Είμαστε εδώ, και το λιμάνι είναι εκεί.
steps.pt: Yes, here you are. We are here, and the port is there.
steps.tts: Ναι, ορίστε. Είμαστε εδώ, και το λιμάνι είναι εκεί.
steps.acao: Two fingers on the paper, εδώ and εκεί. Watch the hand and mark both before you thank them.

steps.es: Πού είναι η στάση; Πού είναι το φαρμακείο; Πού είναι το λιμάνι;
steps.pinyin: POO EE-ne ee STA-see. POO EE-ne to far-ma-KEE-o. POO EE-ne to lee-MA-nee
steps.pt: Shadow the same two words with three completely different places dropped into them.
steps.tts: Πού είναι η στάση; Πού είναι το φαρμακείο; Πού είναι το λιμάνι;

steps.pt: B08 done. One frame, five places, and a follow-up short enough to be answered with a hand.

aprofundar.titulo: Two words, five places, and a smaller answer

secoes.corpo: The place goes in after Πού είναι in its dictionary form — the shape you see on a map, a timetable or a shop front. Nothing about it changes, which is what makes this frame usable while you are still decoding the alphabet: you recognise the word, you say the word. The little words in front of it, η and το, come attached to the noun; learn them as part of the word rather than as a rule.

secoes.titulo: Ask a question whose answer you can hold
secoes.corpo: Πού είναι opens the door and can bring back forty words of street names. The second question is the useful one, and it is designed to be answerable with a gesture: Είναι μακριά; is far or not far. Αριστερά ή δεξιά; puts two options on the table and gets one back. Εδώ; with a finger on the map gets a yes or a correction. You are not shortening the conversation to be polite — you are shortening it so you can act on it.

secoes.titulo: The sign is not the sound
secoes.corpo: Greek road signs are romanised by a national standard used very widely across the country, and the British place-name authority notes plainly that the same standard is a less reliable guide to pronunciation than the older system it replaced. Practical consequence: read the Latin line to identify the place, but say the Greek one. Ρ is an R, Β is a V, Η is an ee, Χ is the sound at the end of Scottish loch. ΒΟΛΟΣ read as Bolos gets you a blank face — and part ten takes the whole set of five apart.

Work on politeness across the two languages describes Greek as oriented to involvement and closeness, and English to distance and non-imposition. That is why the English speaker's padded question — sorry, I don't suppose you could possibly tell me — can land as odd, and why a direct two-word question with a συγγνώμη in front of it reads as completely normal. The mismatch produces two mirror-image misreadings, and knowing that is enough to stop taking either personally.

ευθεία straight on · δεξιά right · αριστερά left · εδώ here · εκεί there · δίπλα next to · απέναντι opposite · κοντά near · μακριά far · πέντε λεπτά με τα πόδια five minutes on foot. Ten words is enough to act on almost any answer you will get.

permissao: You are allowed to ask a two-word question and then interrupt the answer with a smaller one. Nobody is offended by Είναι μακριά; — it is what someone who wants to arrive actually says, and you may use the same two words a dozen times in a day without dressing them up.
espelho: Anyone who has given directions at home knows the moment when the visitor's eyes go flat around the third street name, and knows that the useful thing was the pointed finger. You are just getting to the pointed finger faster.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You ask a two-word question and get a long, fast answer delivered close to your face, with a hand on your arm.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: That was intense — I have annoyed them, or they think I am helpless.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Research comparing the two languages describes Greek politeness as oriented to involvement and closeness, and English politeness to distance and non-imposition. Proximity, volume and taking charge of your problem are the local shape of helpfulness, not of irritation.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stay in it. Let the answer run, then narrow it yourself: Αριστερά ή δεξιά; or Είναι μακριά; Nodding and asking a smaller question is a normal, welcome move here.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You stop reading warmth as pressure, and you leave the exchange with something you can actually walk on.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: This is an orientation described in the research literature, not a personality, and it does not predict any individual. Someone in a hurry is in a hurry, and a short flat answer on a Monday morning means nothing about you.

fichasCulturais.sinal: You read the place name off the road sign, say it out loud, and the person you asked simply does not recognise it.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: My accent is too bad to be understood at all.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The romanisation on the signs is a national transliteration standard used very widely on Greek roads, and the British place-name authority records that it is a less reliable guide to pronunciation than the system it replaced. Reading the Latin line aloud does not reconstruct the Greek word — the letters were chosen to map letters, not sounds.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Use the Latin line to identify the place and the Greek line to say it. Keep four letters in mind: Ρ is R, Β is V, Η is ee, Χ is the loch sound. If it still does not land, point at the word.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: Place names start arriving intact, and you stop attributing to your accent what was really a spelling convention.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not every sign follows the standard: the same authority notes that place names online are not romanised consistently, and older signs, private signs and map apps can disagree with each other. Where they do, the Greek spelling is the one to trust.
